findings.body:
`InsecureSkipVerify: true` is hardcoded on the shared `NewClient()` transport, so **every** environment — including production — will accept any certificate for the ledger host.

Concrete failure mode: an on-path attacker terminates TLS with a bogus cert, then reads or modifies ledger requests/responses with no client-side detection. The staging self-signed rationale and TICKET-77 note do not constrain when this runs; `NewClient()` has no env/config guard.

Gate this behind an explicit non-production config (fail closed in prod), or better: load the staging CA into `tls.Config.RootCAs` so verification stays on. Example shape:

```go
tlsConfig := &tls.Config{MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12}
if cfg.AllowInsecureTLS { // must be false in prod
    tlsConfig.InsecureSkipVerify = true
}
```

summary:
## Verdict

**Do not merge** until TLS verification is environment-gated (or replaced with proper trust for the staging CA). This change disables certificate verification for every caller of `NewClient()`, with no staging/prod split.

## Analysis

`internal/ledger/client.go` sets `tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true}` on the shared HTTP transport. The comment cites a self-signed staging cert and TICKET-77, but `NewClient()` takes no environment, config flag, or base-URL hint — any process that constructs this client (including production) will accept any certificate presented for the ledger host.

Failure mode: an on-path attacker can MITM ledger traffic, read or alter financial payloads, and present an arbitrary cert without detection.

A ticket comment is not a control. Safe options: pin/load the staging CA via `RootCAs`, or set `InsecureSkipVerify` only when an explicit non-prod config value is set and fail closed otherwise.

**Recommendation:** request-changes

verification.reason: `NewClient()` hardcodes `tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true}` with no env/config gate; the patch newly adds this on the shared client transport, so any caller accepts arbitrary certs in all environments.
